drills.q: What's the difference between a fixed-size and variable-size sliding window in terms of what triggers the shrink?
drills.a: Fixed-size: shrink is unconditional, triggered purely by window size exceeding k, one element in one element out. Variable-size: shrink is triggered by a validity constraint being violated (sum, distinct count, frequency), and can require shrinking by more than one element per step.

drills.q: Why is right - left + 1 the correct window length, and what mistake does forgetting the +1 cause?
drills.a: Indices left through right inclusive span (right - left + 1) elements. Forgetting +1 undercounts every window by exactly one, which can make an off-by-one-shorter answer look almost correct on small test cases.

drills.q: Explain why Minimum Window Substring shrinks the window WHILE it's still valid, rather than only shrinking once it becomes invalid.
drills.a: The goal is the SHORTEST valid window, so once a valid window is found you must keep shrinking from the left, recording the length at each step, for as long as it remains valid -- the smallest valid window found during that shrink sequence is a candidate answer. You stop the instant shrinking would make it invalid.

drills.q: A candidate's sliding window solution for 'longest substring with at most K distinct characters' recomputes len(set(window)) on every step by re-scanning the window. What's wrong with this and what's the fix?
drills.a: It reintroduces O(n) work per step, degrading the algorithm to O(n^2) (or O(n * alphabet) if scanning a frequency map). The fix is to maintain an incremental frequency map: increment/decrement counts as characters enter/exit, delete a key when its count hits zero, and track len(map) as a running value updated on each change rather than recomputed.

drills.q: Derive why Sliding Window Maximum needs a monotonic deque rather than a max-heap.
drills.a: A max-heap lets you find the max in O(log n) but doesn't support O(1) removal of an arbitrary element (the one falling out of the window on the left) without lazy deletion bookkeeping. A monotonic decreasing deque of indices instead discards from the back any element that's smaller than a newer element (since it can never be the max while the newer, larger element remains in the window) and discards from the front any index that has fallen outside the window -- both O(1) amortized operations, and the front of the deque is always the current max.

drills.q: Design the decomposition for 'count subarrays with exactly K distinct integers' and explain why a direct sliding window doesn't work for 'exactly K'.
drills.a: exactly(K) = atMost(K) - atMost(K-1). atMost(K) counts, for each right, the number of valid subarrays ending at right with at most K distinct values (computed as right-left+1 once valid), summed over all right. 'Exactly K' isn't monotonic in window size -- growing the window can jump straight from exactly-K to more-than-K without a clean 'exactly K, still exactly K' boundary to slide against, so there's no single validity threshold; decomposing into two monotonic 'at most' problems restores a slidable boundary for each.

drills.q: A rate limiter needs to count events in a rolling 60-second window and reject if the count exceeds a threshold, using an approach analogous to sliding window. What's the naive recomputation failure mode this mirrors, and what's the fix?
drills.a: This mirrors the classic sliding-window anti-pattern of recomputing the count from scratch (re-scanning all stored events) on every incoming event, which degrades to O(n) per event instead of O(1) amortized. The fix, mirroring the incremental-state discipline of sliding window problems, is to maintain a running count and a queue/deque of event timestamps, incrementing on arrival and decrementing (popping from the front) as events age out of the 60-second window, so validity is checked against a running counter, not a full rescan.

drills.q: Why does Minimum Size Subarray Sum break under sliding window if the array can contain negative numbers, and what would you use instead?
drills.a: Sliding window's correctness depends on monotonicity: with all-positive numbers, growing the window strictly increases the sum and shrinking strictly decreases it, so there's a clean boundary to slide against. With negative numbers present, a larger window doesn't guarantee a larger sum, so you can't safely decide whether shrinking or growing moves you toward or away from validity. Prefix sums combined with a sorted structure (or binary search over prefix sums, when applicable) replaces the monotonic pointer argument.
